At length we reduced the weight of the chest by taking out two-thirds of what it held, and could then, with considerable difficulty, lift it clear of the pit. We placed the removed objects among the brambles and stationed the dog to watch them; Jupiter sternly commanded him neither to leave his post on any account nor to make a sound before we returned. Carrying the chest, we hurried homeward and reached the hut safely, though after immense exertion, at one in the morning. In our exhausted condition, human strength could accomplish no more at once. We rested until two and ate supper, then set off immediately for the hills, equipped with three strong sacks fortunately available at the hut. Shortly before four we reached the excavation, shared the remaining plunder between us as evenly as possible, and, leaving the pits open, once more started home. We laid down our golden loads at the hut for the second time just as the earliest pale rays of dawn appeared above the eastern treetops.

We were by now utterly spent, but our overwhelming excitement would not permit proper rest. After three or four hours of troubled sleep, we got up, almost as though by prior agreement, to inspect the treasure.

The chest had been filled to its very brim, and examining its contents occupied the whole day and most of the following night. There had been no semblance of system or arrangement; everything was piled together indiscriminately. When we had carefully sorted it all, our riches proved greater even than we originally imagined. The coins alone amounted to a little above four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, their worth reckoned as nearly as we could from the tables then in use. Not a trace of silver appeared. Everything was old gold, of numerous kinds: French, Spanish, and German pieces, a few English guineas, and certain counters unlike any we had previously encountered. Several coins were exceptionally large and heavy, their surfaces so worn that the inscriptions defeated us. None of the money was American. The gems presented greater difficulty in valuation. There were one hundred and ten diamonds, not a small one among them, and several of extraordinary size and quality; eighteen remarkably lustrous rubies; three hundred and ten emeralds, all exceedingly beautiful; twenty-one sapphires; and one opal. Each stone had been wrenched out of its mounting and tossed loose into the box. The mountings, which we separated from the rest of the gold, seemed to have been battered with hammers, apparently to make recognition impossible.

It was Lady Windermere's final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more packed than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived from the Speaker's formal reception, still wearing their stars and ceremonial ribbons. All the beautiful women had on their finest dresses. At the far end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a stout woman of Tartar appearance with tiny black eyes and magnificent emeralds. She spoke poor French very loudly and laughed extravagantly at everything anyone said to her. It was certainly a remarkable mixture of guests. Splendidly dressed noblewomen chatted pleasantly with fierce Radicals. Popular preachers rubbed shoulders with distinguished skeptics. A whole flock of bishops followed a stout leading opera singer from one room to another. Several members of the Royal Academy stood on the stairs, disguised as artists, and the supper room was said to have been completely full of geniuses at one point. It was, in fact, among Lady Windermere's most successful evenings, and the Princess stayed until almost eleven thirty.

After the Princess left, Lady Windermere returned to the picture gallery. There, a famous political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an offended Hungarian virtuoso. She began talking to the Duchess of Paisley. She looked extraordinarily beautiful, with her magnificent ivory throat, large forget-me-not blue eyes, and thick coils of golden hair. It was pure gold—not the pale straw shade that now claims that lovely name, but the gold found in sunlight or hidden in unusual amber. Her hair framed her face like a saint's, while giving it much of a sinner's attraction. Her character was a curious study. Early in life she had discovered an important truth: nothing resembles innocence so closely as indiscretion. Through a series of reckless adventures, half of them quite harmless, she had won all the freedom allowed to someone with a personality. She had changed husbands more than once; indeed, Debrett's recorded three marriages. But because she had never changed her lover, society had long since stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, had no children, and possessed that excessive love of pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she glanced eagerly around and asked in her clear, low voice, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” the Duchess exclaimed, giving a startled jump.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess. I can't live without him just now.”

“Dear Gladys, you're always so original,” murmured the Duchess, trying to remember what a cheiromantist was and hoping it wasn't the same as a chiropodist.

“He visits regularly twice a week to examine my hand,” Lady Windermere continued, “and says the most interesting things about it.”

My nerves are not suited to such things.”

“But could you feel at ease yourself, passing an entire evening away from the poor child?”

“Yes; his father plainly can, so why should I not? Jemima is exceedingly careful, and could let us know every hour how he went on. Really, Charles might just as well have told his father that we should all be there. I am no more frightened about little Charles now than he is. Yesterday I was terribly frightened, but today the situation is quite changed.”

“Well, provided you think there is still time to send word, why should you not accompany your husband? Let me take charge of little Charles. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot disapprove if I am here with him.”

“Do you mean it?” Mary exclaimed, her eyes lighting up. “Dear me, that is an excellent idea—excellent indeed. Certainly I might as well go, since I serve no purpose at home, do I? It only makes me anxious. Without a mother's feelings, you are far better fitted for the task. You can persuade little Charles to do anything; one word from you is always enough. This will be much better than leaving him with Jemima alone. Oh, I shall definitely go. I am sure I ought to, if possible, just as much as Charles, since they are so very eager for me to meet Captain Wentworth; and I know you have no objection to being alone. Truly a capital suggestion, Anne. I shall tell Charles and prepare immediately. You can summon us in an instant if anything happens, you know, though I expect nothing will occur to frighten you. Be assured I should never leave unless I felt perfectly easy about my darling child.”

A moment later she was knocking at her husband's dressing-room door. Anne followed upstairs in time to hear the entire exchange, which opened with Mary's triumphant announcement:

“I intend to come with you, Charles, since I am no more useful here than you. If I shut myself away with the child for ever, I could not make him do a single thing he disliked. Anne will remain; she has undertaken to stay at home and look after him. It was entirely Anne's suggestion, so I shall accompany you, which is much better, as I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“That is extremely good of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I should be delighted for you to come. Still, it seems a little unfair that she must remain alone at home, nursing our sick child.”
